deep_why: The goal is to recommend items to new users whose preference signals have just arrived, while also learning from the accumulating history of how preferences change over time. The foundational principle is that user preferences follow patterns—some stable across all users (like genre preferences), others unique to individuals (like specific movie tastes)—and that separating these shared patterns from person-specific ones lets a model adapt quickly to new arrivals by borrowing the shared knowledge. Separating them works because new user signals cluster around shared preference dimensions even though individual positions along those dimensions vary widely. This separation holds as long as enough new users arrive to reveal the overlap in pattern space. By maintaining this separation and replaying past examples when learning from new users, the model avoids forgetting the shared patterns it learned before, solving the practical problem of giving accurate recommendations on day one for someone who has just signed up.

The task is teaching a language model which tool to use for a given user request, starting from imperfect training data where some labeled examples are wrong, some tools are rare, and the tool set itself keeps changing. The underlying principle is curriculum learning: humans learn easier skills before harder ones, and arranging training in that order yields faster mastery than random order. This principle applies here because tool selection has layers of difficulty—basic tool-spotting is easier than disambiguating between similar tools—and a model that masters the easy layer first has a foundation to learn finer distinctions on harder examples. By also screening out genuinely wrong labels and starting with high-quality examples, the model builds correct intuitions that survive introduction of noisier data. This approach avoids the trap of memorizing noise, letting the model generalize to new tools and ambiguous queries it has never seen.

Social media events leave traces across images and text that cluster together by theme—a protest leaves a recognizable pattern in both captions and photos—and the goal is to find those clusters without labeled event categories. The core principle is that similarity within a cluster, measured along carefully chosen angles, is stronger than similarity across clusters: if you describe images and text in ways that highlight what makes an event coherent (its theme, its type, what's visually happening), within-cluster pairs will look more alike than random pairs. This principle holds because real events have internal structure—the theme of a protest connects to both its visual markers and how people describe it—and this structure is discoverable without labels by asking a semantic guide (a language model) to describe those dimensions consistently. By forcing the model to make representations that align these descriptions across image and text, the model learns to ignore spurious variation and finds genuine event structure, solving open-world detection without predefined categories.

The goal is to predict purchase conversion during promotional events where buyer behavior shifts sharply compared to regular days. The core principle is stable-plus-flexible modeling: some patterns in user behavior (like how engaged they are) persist across both regular and promotional periods, while others (like price sensitivity) shift with the promotion context. If you can identify which patterns are which, you can reuse the stable ones without retraining from scratch and update only the flexible parts. This separation works because the shift from regular to promotional behavior is partial, not a complete reset—user identity and engagement remain, only their decision-making weights shift. By maintaining this split representation and training a fusion mechanism to know when to trust each part in new promotional contexts, the model avoids catastrophic forgetting of regular-day patterns while staying current on promotional shifts, enabling accurate predictions on a day when behavior is genuinely different from yesterday.

Large recommender systems use multiple retrieval pathways in parallel to cover different user interests, but these pathways overlap: some items multiple retrievers rank highly, giving little new information. The goal is to identify items only earlier retrievers miss and teach the new retriever to specialize in those, improving total system diversity. The principle is that learning is most efficient when training focuses on gaps rather than already-solved cases: a retriever learning from items everyone ignores learns distinctly from one trained on items everyone retrieves. This principle holds because the training signal in recommendation is sparser than in classification—each user sees few items—so wasting signal on consensus items wastes the precious signal that exists. By identifying truly novel items and teaching the retriever to find them specifically, while encouraging it to avoid stealing items the ensemble already ranks well, the system improves coverage without redundancy, delivering more user interests to the ranker and ultimately lifting user transaction rates.

Recommender systems transfer knowledge between product categories (like books and movies) to handle data sparsity, but category-specific words in product descriptions can have different meanings in different categories, breaking knowledge transfer. The goal is to identify which words are truly universal, which are category-specific, and which are category-independent but mean different things across categories. The principle is that meaning depends on context: the word 'action' means 'fast-paced narrative' in movies but 'physical interaction' in video games, and mistaking these for the same concept causes negative transfer. Categorizing words by how concentrated they are within one category versus spread across categories reveals these meanings: concentrated words are category-specific, widespread words are universal, and words somewhere in between may carry hidden domain-specific weight within their category. By respecting these boundaries and connecting only universal knowledge across categories, the model reuses genuine shared patterns while avoiding poisoned transfer from false synonyms, improving recommendations in sparse categories without hurting rich ones.

Computing how central each node is in a social network (by the Katz measure) exactly requires tracking influence paths of all lengths, which explodes in cost as networks grow. The goal is to approximate this ranking efficiently on massive graphs. The principle is random walks: if you repeatedly start from a node, take random steps following edges, and count how often you reach other nodes, the hit frequency approximates their true centrality ranking. This approximation works because the random walk process naturally weights paths by their frequency and accessibility—common paths get explored more often—which aligns with how Katz centrality mathematically weights paths, just computed probabilistically rather than algebraically. By running many independent random walks in parallel, computers working on different walks simultaneously, the computation becomes faster by orders of magnitude while maintaining ranking accuracy. This approach trades numerical precision in individual scores for speed and parallelizability, solving the practical problem of identifying influential users in networks too large for exact computation.

Search results pages are no longer linear lists but complex layouts where item position, neighbors, and visual design all influence clicks and purchases, yet standard ranking models optimize for position only. The goal is to optimize the entire page experience, including long-term satisfaction like repeat purchases weeks later. The principle is causal effect: measuring what would happen if you placed item A in location 1 versus location 2 requires isolating the effect of placement from all other differences between users who see each position. Quasi-experimental data—users assigned to pages slightly differently—reveals these effects if analyzed carefully. This principle applies because page position affects both immediate click behavior and long-term trust and discovery: a well-placed item may not be clicked today but discover a shopper to a brand they visit later. By using causal reasoning to measure long-term impact and then optimizing page layout for it rather than clicks alone, the model captures the true value of placement and visual emphasis, solving the business problem of sustainable shopper satisfaction rather than optimizing narrow short-term clicks.

Generative recommenders that process long user histories produce better recommendations but are slow because they must read and process every past item. The goal is to compress history without losing quality. The principle is that item categories summarize: a user who clicked sports, sports, adventure, adventure has interests in sports and adventure, and those two categories capture their pattern better than six individual item reads. This principle holds because category membership is stable across time while specific items create noise—whether the user clicked 'basketball' or 'soccer' matters less than that they like sports. By grouping items into their category and running the recommender on one instance per category instead of all items, the model reduces computation while preserving the signal about what the user cares about. Experiments show this works as well as much longer histories because the model extracts the true underlying interest without the redundancy of repeated category exposure, solving the deployment problem of making recommendations fast without sacrificing accuracy.

Estimating how an individual would respond to an intervention (like a price discount) from network data is hard because people influence each other and confounding factors drive both the decision to intervene and the response. The goal is to disentangle these causes. The principle is that hidden factors divide into roles: some create instruments that justify intervention choices without affecting outcomes (like budget availability), some cause bias by influencing both intervention and outcome (like user wealth), and some affect outcomes only given the intervention. If you can identify these three roles separately, you can measure the intervention effect by adjusting for the confounding factors while preserving the instrumental factors that made the intervention natural. This principle holds because causal structure is identifiable when the roles reflect genuinely different information flows in the data. By learning representations that capture these distinct factors and regularizing them to maintain separation, the model recovers the true causal effect sizes even when people influence each other, solving the core inference problem of learning how to optimally target interventions from observational network data.

Detecting anomalies in multivariate time series where multiple measurements evolve together is challenging because errors in one measurement compound errors in others if you train the model on all measurements at once. The goal is to improve detection by focusing the model on one target measurement at a time. The principle is concentration: a model trained to minimize error on a single target distributes learning effort entirely on that target, whereas a model trained on many targets dilutes effort across them. This principle applies because each measurement can have anomalies at different times and severities, so a model predicting multiple outputs simultaneously must compromise, fitting some measurements better and others worse. By training separate models for each measurement while only including measurements similar to the target as inputs, the model benefits from related patterns without spreading its error budget. This focused training, combined with access to neighbor patterns that often show anomalies together, gives each model the signal concentration and relevant context it needs to detect subtle anomalies, dramatically improving detection rates on real industrial sensor data.

Information extraction from text using large language models breaks down when different tasks define entities differently—a 'person' means something different in biography extraction versus clinical notes—and training on multiple definitions causes the model to forget how to handle each one correctly. The goal is to reuse the model's general language understanding while delegating schema-specific mapping to lightweight task-specific models. The principle is separation of concerns: understanding language and identifying named entities is a general skill that applies to all schemas, whereas mapping identified entities to a particular schema's categories is task-specific. These skills are separable because you can identify where 'John Smith' appears in text without knowing whether to call it a 'person', 'subject', or 'entity'; the category assignment is a separate decision. By training the large model only on the general skill (identifying and understanding spans) across all tasks simultaneously, then training lightweight specialists for each schema, the model avoids forgetting one schema when learning another and keeps general ability sharp. This division lets the large model reuse its understanding broadly while allowing each schema to define its own categories, solving the problem of building extraction systems that handle multiple conflicting schemas in production.

Self-training for entity recognition amplifies small amounts of labeled data by using a model's own predictions on unlabeled data as new training examples, but the model often predicts wrong and those wrong predictions become training signal, causing errors to compound. The goal is to filter out incorrect predictions before adding them as training data. The principle is that large language models have rich knowledge about text and entities that a pure machine learning model lacks, and they can judge whether a predicted entity makes sense given the text's context and actual patterns in the training data. This principle applies because the language model's knowledge comes from diverse text and is orthogonal to the biases the specialized entity recognizer develops. By asking the language model to validate predictions using task rules the language model itself extracted from the labeled data, combined with multiple agreement signals, the model filters pseudo-labels to keep only plausible ones. This careful filtering breaks the error amplification cycle of standard self-training, solving the practical problem of learning entity boundaries accurately from few labeled examples and plentiful unlabeled text.

This is a tutorial paper surveying retrieval-augmented generation systems that incorporate structured data like tables, graphs, and hierarchies rather than just flat text. While a tutorial offering structural perspective on RAG design patterns rather than a single method, the underlying principle across all structured RAGs is that structure constrains retrieval: knowing that data lives in a table means you search columns and rows following their edges, knowing it's a graph means you traverse connections, knowing it's a tree means you exploit parent-child relationships. This constraint is sound because external knowledge that is structured does have those boundaries and relationships, and respecting them prevents nonsensical retrieval like matching unrelated tables rows or following broken graph edges. By tailoring retrieval algorithms to the actual structure of each knowledge type rather than treating all knowledge as unstructured text, these systems make fewer spurious retrievals, answer more precisely, and remain more trustworthy in safety-critical scenarios where confidently wrong answers are worse than no answer. The tutorial synthesizes how structure fundamentally improves retrieval quality and safety.

Breaking a matrix into its building blocks (rank-1 components) typically uses numerical algorithms with fixed rules for when to stop, but these rules don't adapt to different data characteristics like noise. The goal is to replace those fixed rules with intelligent agents that can decide adaptively when to stop. The principle is hierarchical understanding: when you peel away one rank-1 layer and look at what remains, you can see if it's noise or signal by asking whether its structure is visually coherent—random noise looks like chaos, true signal looks like a pattern. If you can describe what you see in the remaining matrix to an agent and ask it to judge coherence, the agent applies its visual judgment instead of a formula. This principle works because visual coherence is a proxy for presence of real signal that generalizes across different noise levels and matrix types, whereas fixed thresholds are tuned for one noise level and fail on others. By alternating between a language model that proposes the next rank-1 extraction and a vision agent that judges whether the remainder still contains signal worth extracting, the system adapts extraction to the actual structure present, achieving threshold-free deflation that beats fixed-rule algorithms.
